column5: God teaches Ephraim to walk
column6: The commentary defines Rab as raising a child through successive stages; Hosea says God taught Ephraim to walk and took the child by the arms, presenting divine care as hands-on early nurture.

column5: loving bonds and feeding
column6: The commentary links mercy with beneficence and raising a child toward completion; Hosea says God led Israel with loving bonds, bent down, and fed them. The middle image is rendered either as lifting an infant to the cheek or lifting a yoke from the jaws, so both readings remain visible.

column5: God carries Israel as a father carries a son
column6: The commentary moves from the womb to a child raised by a household; Moses recalls God carrying Israel through the wilderness as a man carries his son, a direct parental-care image.

column5: God who gave birth is forgotten
column6: The commentary surrounds nurture with womb and parental care; Moses’ song accuses Israel of forgetting the Rock who gave birth to them, reversing the expected child’s response to the one who formed and raised them.

column5: womb and mother’s breasts
column6: The commentary calls the womb a child’s first home and describes subsequent nurture; the psalmist says God took him from the womb and made him secure at his mother’s breasts.

column5: cast from the womb toward God
column6: The commentary’s womb image is a home for the child; the psalm says the speaker was cast upon God from birth and relied on God from his mother’s womb, extending the image from maternal shelter to divine care.

column5: God supports from the womb
column6: The commentary pictures mercy as care that begins in the womb and continues through a child’s growth; the psalmist says he has leaned on God from birth and was taken from the womb by God.

column5: children as fruit of the womb
column6: The commentary begins its frame with the womb as the child’s home; the psalm calls children an inheritance from God and the fruit of the womb a reward, assigning value to the life that grows there.

column5: a weaned child with its mother
column6: The commentary describes a child’s growth inside a home and the transition toward completion; the psalm compares its quieted soul to a weaned child beside its mother, where dependence has changed but maternal closeness remains.

column5: formed in the mother’s womb
column6: The commentary makes the womb a place where a child grows and is formed; the psalm says God knit the speaker together in his mother’s womb, locating divine making within that home.

column5: n-ʿ-m / pleasant kinship
column6: The commentary labels Arabic ن ع م and glosses it with raising children in comfort; Hebrew naʿim is a cognate meaning pleasant, used here of brothers dwelling together, so the source’s comfort image meets a concrete kin household.

column5: q-w-m / children rise in the household
column6: The commentary labels Arabic ق و م for the one who keeps household affairs standing; Hebrew qûm is a cognate used when the woman’s children rise to call her blessed, placing the root in a household where her care is recognized.

column5: Israel loved as a child and called out of Egypt
column6: The commentary recounts Moses’ threatened infancy and return to his mother; Hosea depicts Israel collectively as God’s child, loved and called out of Egypt, turning the Exodus setting into a parent-child relation.

column5: shepherd carries lambs and leads nursing ewes
column6: The commentary describes the home as a place of protection and sustenance; Isaiah pictures God gathering lambs in his arms, carrying them close, and gently leading nursing mothers.

column5: children nursed, carried, and comforted
column6: The commentary links the womb to a child’s home and later nurture; Isaiah depicts Jerusalem’s children nursing, being carried on her hip, and bounced on her knees, giving several concrete stages of maternal care.

column5: Hannah continues to provide after weaning
column6: The commentary treats nurturing as continuing beyond birth and recognizes care by someone outside the child’s daily home; although Samuel serves at Shiloh, his mother brings him a small robe each year.

column5: Elijah returns a son to his mother
column6: The commentary recounts Moses being restored to his mother after separation; Elijah brings the widow’s revived son down and gives him to her, a distinct Hebrew Bible reunion scene.

column5: weaning marks a changed stage
column6: The commentary describes raising a child from state to state; Abraham’s feast on the day Isaac is weaned marks the end of nursing and a public transition in the child’s life.

column5: a mother and child expelled from home
column6: The commentary presents the home as the child’s place of nurture and protection; Sarah demands Hagar and her son be sent away, showing the contrary case of a household withdrawing that shelter.

column5: Moses hidden before being sent onto the river
column6: The commentary’s Qur’anic account begins with God directing Moses’ mother to nurse him and then place him in the water; Exodus first says she hides the newborn for three months, a distinct step before the basket episode.

column5: Pharaoh’s daughter finds the infant
column6: The commentary says the Pharaoh household takes Moses but emphasizes the sister’s proposal and his return to his mother; Exodus identifies Pharaoh’s daughter as the one who finds the basket and sends her servant to fetch it.

column5: kinship made through joined life
column6: The commentary explains “rahim” kinship as relatives who came from one womb; Genesis gives a different foundation for family relation, saying husband and wife become one flesh, adding a bond formed through shared life rather than birth.

column5: train a child in a way
column6: The commentary defines tarbiya as bringing a thing through stages toward completion; Proverbs tells an adult to train a child in the way he should go, relating instruction to the child’s later life.

column5: discipline as parental care
column6: The commentary portrays raising a child as purposeful formation; Proverbs connects a parent’s love with diligent correction, a sharper form of nurture than the commentary’s gentler household image.

column5: q-w-m is not the link; parental discipline is
column6: The commentary defines Rab as raising a child toward completion; Proverbs says the Lord corrects the one he loves as a father corrects a son, supplying a direct Hebrew parental-formation motif.

column5: Christian reading of Proverbs’ fatherly discipline
column6: The commentary describes nurture as formation toward completion; Hebrews quotes the father-son discipline saying from Proverbs and interprets hardship as the Lord’s treatment of children he receives, giving correction a filial meaning.

column5: parents give good gifts to children
column6: The commentary joins mercy with doing good and the Lord with a child’s nurturer; Jesus argues from human parents giving good gifts to their children toward the heavenly Father’s greater generosity.

column5: nourishing and cherishing one’s own
column6: The commentary describes a home that nurtures and protects its members; Ephesians says no one hates his own body but nourishes and cherishes it, then uses that care to explain Christ’s care for the church.

column5: a father addresses his children
column6: The commentary pairs the mother’s womb and a father’s role in raising a child; Paul recalls exhorting and encouraging each Thessalonian as a father addresses his own children.

column5: parental guidance toward a worthy life
column6: The commentary says upbringing leads step by step toward completion; Paul says he urged the community to live worthily of God, like a father guiding children toward their calling.

column5: womb and breasts named as maternal blessing
column6: The commentary explicitly develops the womb, the child’s home, and the nurturing relation; a woman blesses the womb that bore Jesus and the breasts that nursed him.

column5: Jesus redirects blessing to hearing the word
column6: The commentary connects maternal nurture with the teacher who feeds learners; Jesus answers the womb-and-breast blessing by calling blessed those who hear God’s word and keep it, shifting the measure toward instruction and response.

column5: the disciple takes Mary into his home
column6: The commentary describes kinship through a shared womb and care within a household; after entrusting his mother to the disciple, Jesus’ words lead the disciple to take her into his own home, making protection concrete.

column5: Jesus takes children in his arms
column6: The commentary says mercy especially bends toward the weak; Jesus takes little children in his arms, lays hands on them, and blesses them after the disciples tried to keep them away.

column5: a child moves in the womb
column6: The commentary’s central image is the womb as the child’s home; Elizabeth says the child in her womb leapt when Mary’s greeting reached her, a specific intrauterine scene.

column5: labor pain and joy after birth
column6: The commentary recalls pain in the womb after delivery; Jesus compares grief followed by joy to a woman distressed in labor who rejoices after her child is born, preserving the passage’s focus on labor and birth rather than postpartum illness.

column5: adoption into God’s family
column6: The commentary notes a spouse raising a child who is not biologically theirs; Paul says Christ redeems those under the law so they may receive adoption as children, applying household adoption to believers.

column5: father’s concrete duties to a son
column6: The commentary’s Rab raises and teaches a child; Kiddushin lists a father’s obligations to his son, including teaching Torah and a trade, making nurture a set of practical responsibilities.
